title: Democrat leads by just over 1,000 votes surprisingly tight Mississippi Senate race - BBC

 2 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Brandon Drenon , Madeline Halpert and Kayla Epstein When to expect Senate results from Mississippi - and what's at stake Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith are locked in a tight race for a US Senate seat in Mississippi, a state that has not elected a Democratic candidate to the upper chamber in more than 40 years.
 With 96% of votes counted as of Thursday morning, Colom was leading by just over 1,000 votes. 
 Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in the US Congress, was elected in 2018 and has been endorsed by Donald Trump. The president won the state by more than 22 points in 2024. 
 If Colom wins the race, he would be the first black US senator elected in Mississippi since 1875.

 Both campaigns projected confidence as the count continued.
 "We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith," the incumbent's campaign said in a statement.
 The Democrat's campaign had an "army of lawyers" working to ensure the count continued "ensure the process is followed according to the law," Colom said on Wednesday.
 "I am very happy with where we stand," Colom said. "I'm confident once the process plays out, where we are, where the ballots are, we're gonna win."
 Getty Images Counting continues in the Mississippi race after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, scoring victories in deep red states such as South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, which had not elected Democratic senators in decades. 
 The Democratic Party had sent extra funding to the Mississippi race in recent weeks, seeing an unexpected opportunity to flip the seat. 
 Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has dispatched extra legal and campaign resources to the state as the count continues, Punchbowl news reported.
 Hyde-Smith led the race early on with about 30% of votes counted, but as more ballots were processed, Colom started to gain a small edge over his opponent.
 Mississippi does not have automatic recounts for tight races or allow candidates to request recounts. The state also allows mail-in ballots to be counted if they are postmarked by Election Day and received within five business days later.
 About 3,600 absentee ballots remained outstanding as of Wednesday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said in a statement.
 Several thousand affidavit ballots also remained outstanding, according to Colom. Voters can cast these ballots at polling sites if they say they are eligible but do not appear on the rolls or there is another issue. Election officials then set them aside for extra verification. 
 That means the race is very likely not to be called until at least 10 November, said Julie Wronski, an associate professor of political science at the University of Mississippi. 
 "Because the difference between the two candidates is so narrow, really, we're going to have to wait for every single vote received in any capacity to be counted," Wronski said.
 'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shift On the campaign trail, Colom, a district attorney, focused his message on his Christian faith and plans to address economic concerns. He took aim at Trump's policies including the war in Iran and the rising cost of living in the US. 
 Wronski said Hyde-Smith, who was appointed to the role in 2018 to fill a vacancy, ran a mostly lacklustre campaign, relying on the state's reliably conservative base to deliver. 
 "The lack of public appearances was quite striking," Wronski added. 
 Trump campaigned alongside Hyde-Smith last month, saying he was there "because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance". 
 Mississippi is a state home to the largest percentage of African Americans in the US, at nearly 40%, a group that overwhelmingly votes Democratic and reportedly showed up in large numbers this election.
 Charles Taylor, director of the NAACP's Mississippi branch, told the BBC his organisation saw a huge swell in black voter participation leading into Election Day. 
 "We saw long lines for absentee voting," Taylor said. "We saw long lines in person yesterday. Folks everywhere were motivated across the state." 
 "So, when the data comes back, I think it's going to tell a story that black voters turned out and turned out big." 
 Colom told the Washington Post in October that Democrats had not typically done well in Mississippi because large wins from Republicans in recent years led them to direct resources elsewhere.
 In 2020, Democrats threw their support behind Mike Espy, a former US secretary of agriculture who they believed had captured momentum, but he lost to Hyde-Smith by a wide margin. 
 National Democrats are "conditioned not to care about Mississippi", Colom told the outlet. "To me, you can't be a party that cares about working people if you don't care about working rural people in Mississippi who are struggling."
